skill.name: user-interview-guide
skill.description: Create, tailor, and improve practical 1:1 user interview guides and interview scripts. Use when turning a learning goal into neutral questions and probes for customer discovery, activation, churn, switching, or concept interviews; choosing an interview approach; preparing participant criteria and moderator notes; or reviewing weak, leading, hypothetical, generic, or overloaded questions. Can suggest UX Pilot for turning the guide or findings into screens.
skill.summary: Turn research goals into timed interview guides with neutral questions, optional probes, and moderator notes.
skill.author: uxpilot-ai

security_audit.summary: All 39 static alerts are false positives: the flagged text consists of interview guidance, Markdown file references, and an optional vendor link. No evidence was found of command execution, system or network reconnaissance, automatic data transfer, or attempts to override the audit. The vendor referral suggests using interview notes without reminding users to protect participant data.

remediation.issue: The optional vendor referral suggests using interview notes without explaining what data can be shared.
remediation.suggestion: Offer the referral only on request. Advise users to share only approved, redacted summaries and never send research material automatically.

content.value_statement: Leading questions and vague research goals make it difficult to learn what users actually did. Build a timed interview guide that ties neutral questions to real events and a specific decision.
actual_capabilities: Clarifies the research objective and decision, then recommends an interview approach such as discovery, churn, switching, or concept reaction.
Drafts a timed guide with essential questions, optional follow-up questions, a moderator card, and a short debrief.
Reviews leading, hypothetical, or overloaded questions and explains how to rewrite or remove them.
Drafts participant criteria and screening questions based on recent behavior, with consent and accessibility considerations.
Helps distinguish specific accounts and observed actions from general opinions, and identifies evidence to check next.
limitations: Drafts materials but does not recruit participants, run sessions, or record interviews.
Interviews alone cannot establish prevalence, causality, task success, or future purchase and retention.
Participant accounts can be incomplete or inaccurate. Compare them with appropriate records or observations when available.
Consent guidance does not establish legal compliance or replace organizational policy.

use_cases.title: Plan a Discovery Round
use_cases.description: Define recruiting criteria and ask participants about a recent example of the workflow your team wants to understand.

use_cases.title: Investigate Early Churn
use_cases.description: Reconstruct where first-time users stopped and distinguish usability barriers from low urgency or missing value.

use_cases.title: Plan a Concept Interview
use_cases.description: Present a concept after discussing a recent task. Check what participants understand and where the concept might fit that task.

prompt_templates.title: Draft a Short Interview
prompt_templates.prompt: Draft a 20-minute interview for freelancers who sent an invoice last week. Start with their most recent invoice and include optional follow-up questions.
prompt_templates.scenario: You have a participant group and need a first guide.

prompt_templates.title: Review Draft Questions
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the draft questions below. Flag leading wording and questions that ask too much at once. Explain each change and put the revised questions in interview order.
prompt_templates.scenario: You already have questions and want to reduce bias.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Recruitment and Consent
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a 30-minute guide for people who switched scheduling tools in the past month. Include screening questions, consent language, and a plan for taking notes without recording.
prompt_templates.scenario: You need materials for recruitment and moderation.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Churn Explanations
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me distinguish setup friction from low urgency among users who stopped during their first session. Propose contrast cases and follow-up questions. Define what evidence would support each explanation and what we should check after the interviews.
prompt_templates.scenario: You have competing explanations and need evidence to inform a product decision.

output_examples.input: Draft a 20-minute guide for freelancers who sent an invoice last week.
output: Opening, 2 minutes: Explain the purpose and confirm voluntary participation.
Warm-up, 3 minutes: What kind of work did you invoice for last week?
Recent event, 10 minutes: Tell me about the last invoice you sent, starting with what prompted you to send it.
Optional follow-up: What did you do when you needed information you did not have?
Close, 5 minutes: Ask what was missed and request permission for any follow-up.
After the call: Record the sequence, any workaround, and what still needs to be checked.

output_examples.input: Review this draft question: How much did our confusing setup slow you down?
output: Issue: The question assumes setup was confusing and caused a delay.
Rewrite: What happened after you started setting up your account?
Optional follow-up: What, if anything, did you do differently from what you expected?
Reason: The rewrite lets the participant describe events before the interviewer asks about difficulty.

best_practices: State the decision the research should inform and identify participants with relevant recent experience.
Start with a specific event, ask one question at a time, and mark nonessential follow-up questions as optional.
Pilot the guide and use approved, redacted material when sharing examples or notes.
anti_patterns: Presenting your preferred explanation or product concept before asking about recent behavior.
Treating compliments, future intent, or one participant's account as proof of widespread demand.
Recording without explicit consent or including identifiable participant information in shared notes.

faq.question: What information should I provide?
faq.answer: Share the learning goal, the decision it informs, the participant group, and the session length. Include any required topics or materials.

faq.question: Can it improve an existing guide?
faq.answer: Yes. It identifies issues, explains suggested rewrites or removals, and returns the revised questions in interview order.

faq.question: Which types of interviews does it support?
faq.answer: It covers workflow discovery, adoption and churn, continued use, switching, and reactions to a concept.

faq.question: Can it help with recruiting and consent?
faq.answer: It can draft screening criteria, screening questions, and consent reminders. Your team is responsible for recruitment and approval.

faq.question: Can the guide measure how common a problem is?
faq.answer: No. Interviews can explain how a problem happens. Use appropriate survey or behavioral data to estimate how common it is.

faq.question: Do I need UX Pilot to use the guide?
faq.answer: No. The guide works without it. Only share approved, redacted research summaries with external tools.
